query: For a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, whose elevated-temperature mechanical performance remains unestablished when titanium and nickel serve as primary constituents rather than additions, what single testable intervention hypothesis could produce better mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing than the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, mechanism, predicted relative outcome, applicable composition and test-regime boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Processing a titanium–nickel high-entropy alloy in an ultra‐high purity (oxygen‐ and nitrogen‐free) environment will reduce interstitial impurity uptake, thereby minimizing impurity‐induced phase segregation and softening at high temperatures. This intervention acts in part by preserving severe lattice distortion in the solid-solution, maintaining effective dislocation pinning, which should yield superior high-temperature strength and creep resistance compared to the same HEA made under conventional atmospheric conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase solid-solution high-entropy alloy in which titanium and nickel are primary constituents, fabricated by conventional arc-melting that typically incurs trace levels of oxygen and nitrogen interstitials.
generation.intervention: Adopt an ultra-high vacuum or rigorously controlled inert gas processing route (with appropriate gettering if needed) during melting and solidification to minimize oxygen and nitrogen contamination.
generation.conditions: Tested under high-temperature mechanical regimes (e.g., tensile or creep tests at service-relevant temperatures) on samples that are otherwise compositionally identical but differ in impurity content.
generation.structural_mediator: A cleaner solid-solution microstructure with reduced interstitials prevents the formation of deleterious segregated phases or precipitate-free zones at grain boundaries that would otherwise lower the solid-solution strengthening effect.
generation.mechanism: Reducing impurity uptake prevents local depletion of strengthening solutes and avoids impurity-induced phase segregation during high-temperature exposure, thereby maintaining severe lattice distortion and effective dislocation pinning which enhances load-bearing capacity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The ultra-high purity processed alloy will exhibit higher yield strength and improved creep resistance at elevated temperatures, along with a microstructure showing fewer signs of nanoscale phase segregation compared to the conventionally processed counterpart.
generation.baseline: The performance of the same Ti–Ni HEA fabricated via standard processing (arc melting under conventional atmospheres, with typical oxygen/nitrogen pickup) without enhanced impurity control.
generation.boundary: This benefit is predicted to hold in the high-temperature regime (approximately 700°C–1000°C) where impurity effects are most deleterious to solid-solution strengthening; effects outside this temperature range or for multiphase materials remain uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the mechanical improvement is uncertain and may depend on the residual impurity levels and subtle processing parameters. Further quantification is required to establish the exact performance gains.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Ti–Ni-based HEA samples: one using conventional arc-melting in a standard atmosphere (control) and the other using an ultra-high purity processing route (intervention). Subject both sets to identical post-solidification heat treatments and then perform elevated-temperature mechanical tests (e.g., tensile tests and creep tests at 700–1000°C). In parallel, conduct high-resolution microstructural analyses (using TEM, EDS) to quantify impurity levels and detect signs of phase segregation.
measurements: Grain boundary and matrix impurity concentration (O, N)
Evidence of nanoscale phase segregation or precipitate formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ultra-high purity processed samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in elevated-temperature mechanical properties (e.g., yield strength, creep resistance) or if they exhibit similar levels of phase segregation and impurity content compared to conventionally processed samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are emerging materials with potential for use under extreme conditions. As a newly developed material system, a comprehensive understanding of their long-term stability under potential service temperatures remains to be established. This study examined a titanium-vanadium-niobium-tantalum alloy, a promising RHEA known for its superior high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility. Using a combination of advanced analytical microscopies, Calculation of Phase Diagrams (CALPHAD) software, and nanoindentation, we investigated the evolution of its microstructure and mechanical properties upon aging at 700°C. Trace interstitials such as oxygen and nitrogen, initially contributing to solid solution strengthening, promote phase segregation during thermal aging. As a result of the depletion of solute interstitials within the metal matrix, a progressive softening is observed in the alloy as a function of aging time. This study, therefore, underscores the need for a better control of impurities in future development and application of RHEAs.
